results.question: What does the book say about making your own chroma keyer?
results.answer:
The book's take is two-sided: it spells out a concrete do-it-yourself recipe, then freely admits the result will probably be more trouble than it's worth. Unlike the homemade **luma keyer** it builds in Section 2.1.3, where a clever build can beat the basic tools, the author says a homemade chroma keyer is likely just an interesting exercise in testing your mettle, because an off-the-shelf chroma keyer is hard to improve upon [S2].

The recipe is simple. Start with an operation that converts the RGB image to HSV, then pipe the HSV image into a color curve: the RED curve now holds Hue data, the GREEN curve holds Saturation, and the BLUE curve holds Value (brightness) [S1]. You adjust the three curves to include or exclude the hue, saturation, and value ranges of the target object, and the book suggests testing your work on the included `WWW Chroma key target.tif`, a colorful image meant for pulling keys on various parts of the picture [S5]. A second variant, the 3D color keyer in 2.2.3, works on different principles entirely: rather than converting to HSV, it keys on the specific color of the item of interest by plotting the backing pixels in the RGB color cube, which the book describes as a "grossly simplified version of the operating principles of Primatte" [S7].

For context, the book defines a chroma keyer as one that takes RGB and converts it internally to HSV (or HSL), because saturation is not an attribute directly readable from RGB [S13]. A starting pixel value sets the center of the key, separate ranges are set for Hue, Saturation, and Value, pixels inside the ranges go to white and those outside go to black, and tolerance controls on each setting soften the matte's edges [S13].

Practically, the book's advice is to try a chroma key first because it is quick, but to switch to a color difference key if the edges aren't good enough, since it will usually give much nicer edges [S15]. One terminology caveat it flags: most greenscreen keyers on the market (Keylight, Ultimatte) are really color difference keyers, not chroma keyers in the strict HSV sense — Primatte is the notable exception, being a sophisticated three-dimensional chroma keyer [S4].

results.question: What does the book say about nonsquare pixels?
results.answer:
Nonsquare (rectangular) pixels are pixels whose width and height aren't equal, with the width-to-height relationship expressed as the **pixel aspect ratio**; a normal computer monitor's square pixels have a PAR of 1:1 [S1][S3][S4]. The book's core point is that nonsquare pixels exist because the aspect ratio of the image *as displayed* can differ from the aspect ratio of the original digital image — so calling a system "nonsquare" describes the display geometry, not the actual shape of pixels on your monitor [S2][S5].

## Where they come from

- **Anamorphic/squeezed film formats** — like Cinemascope's dramatic 2:1 squeeze — distort the image optically; these are called "squeezed" or "anamorphic" formats because film has no identifiable pixels [S6][S8].
- **Standard-definition video** — NTSC-DV at 720×480 and PAL-DV at 720×576 — uses rectangular pixels, while HD, graphics software, and computer monitors use square pixels [S9].
- **The classic example** — NTSC analog video has a PAR of 10:11, so pixels are slightly taller than wide; a perfectly round circle sent to NTSC without correction displays as an ellipse, stretched 11/10 vertically [S11].

## Author's stance and practical advice

The author is careful to dispel a common misconception: the temporary "unsqueeze" some systems apply to display nonsquare-pixel footage is a geometric transformation of the *display only* — the underlying image data isn't modified [S5]. Crucially, you must not confuse pixel aspect ratio with image aspect ratio; they're independent numbers [S7][S11]. That's why the author's strongest warning is about compositing transforms: rotating an element *without* accounting for the squeeze produces visibly wrong results — the correct procedure is to **unsqueeze, rotate, then resqueeze** along the x-axis [S10]. The takeaway is to double-check any operation when working in nonsquare-pixel formats, since subtle distortion (even a 5° rotation) can sneak into the final result [S10].

results.question: What does the book say about miscellaneous drawing tips?
results.answer:
Francis Glebas's *Directing the Story* carries two short lists of miscellaneous drawing tips [S3][S6], and they all point one direction: a drawing's job is to communicate clearly and vividly. The recurring themes are clarity of intent, boldness of line, and expressive, purposeful poses.

- Draw for **clarity** — one idea per sketch — and highlight the important idea of the sketch while subordinating everything else to it [S3][S6].
- Have something to say in your image; don't doodle [S3].
- Don't get too clever: tricky camera angles usually just make the drawing ambiguous [S6].
- Don't be afraid to redraw, searching for the best solution to tell the story; if part of a drawing doesn't work, cut it out and rework it [S3].
- Play straight lines against curves for interest, and use straight line symbols for stretches, bent line symbols for squashes [S3][S6].
- Avoid **symmetry** — it's boring and makes drawings look cut out; use angles to build dynamic asymmetry [S6].
- Draw borders so you have to compose to them [S6].
- When drawing eyes, darken the pupils [S3].
- Draw bold and expressive [S6].
- Show how the character feels: feel the pose and the emotion in your own body as you draw [S6].
- A person is always doing something, so express the purpose and experience the pose kinetically [S6].
- Watch the body's landmarks where bones reach the surface, such as the hipbones and ribs [S6].

These fit with the advice around them in the same book — test a drawing by blackening it in to make sure the silhouette still reads, keep decoration inside the main outline so drawings don't get busy [S1], and draw bold (grease pencil, marker, or 2B pencil) so drawings read from across the room, numbering them as you go [S2]. The rationale is stated plainly in the "Show and Tell" section: draw attention to one idea at a time, just as you would when speaking [S7].

results.question: What does the book say about transcoding versus color rerendering?
results.answer:
The VES Handbook frames the choice as a question of how dissimilar the two display environments are: **transcoding** handles the easy case where displays differ only in their color primaries, while **color rerendering** is the recommended solution when the displays' contrast, white levels, or viewing conditions are grossly dissimilar [S1][S2].

For transcoding, the displays are assumed to share black levels, white luminance, viewing conditions, and gamma — only the primary chromaticities differ. In that case the encoded colors can be re-targeted by linearizing the first display's encoded RGB values, converting them to CIE XYZ, converting those XYZ values to the second display's RGB, and reimposing the encoding nonlinearity [S2]. Because appearance is already matched, the transform is purely mathematical.

Color rerendering is a deeper operation. Any color rendering implicitly or explicitly done for the first display is first undone, and then the non-color-rendered CIE XYZ values are color rendered for the second display [S1]. Here "color rendering" means transforming an image to account for differences in viewing environment — for example, a scene shot in bright sunlight reproduced on an office monitor whose peak white is hundreds of times dimmer [S4]. That's why it's the better route when viewing conditions genuinely diverge: a simple encoding swap can't preserve appearance.

| Aspect | Transcoding | Color rerendering |
|---|---|---|
| **When to use** | Displays similar (black level, white luminance, gamma, viewing conditions); primaries differ | Contrast, white levels, or viewing conditions grossly dissimilar |
| **What it does** | Linearize → XYZ → sRGB-style re-encode for display 2 | Undo first display's color rendering, then re-render XYZ for display 2 |
| **Complexity** | Simpler, encoding-level operation | More involved, reverses then reapplies appearance rendering |
| **Workflow note** | Preserves the intended look because displays are near-equivalent | Necessary when appearance would otherwise be broken by the environment change |

The practical implication is that transcoding is the low-cost path when you're moving between similar displays, but it stops being valid once the viewing environment shifts — which is consistent with the handbook's broader point that color rendering is easier to do downstream than to undo if it was baked into a non-raw format [S6].

results.question: What does the book say about FACE OFF?
results.answer:
The corpus doesn’t discuss the film *Face/Off* (John Woo, 1997) or any single entry titled “FACE OFF.” The only usage in the retrieved books is the literal combat term — the face-off as the standoff that opens a fight.

In **How to Draw Manga Martial Arts and Combat Sports**, the face-off is the precise opening moment of a match: opponents stand facing each other at a distance roughly equal to where the tips of their bamboo swords touch, then squat with thighs open in the *Sonkyo* (knee-bend squat), rise into the ready position, and the match begins from there [S3]. The fight choreography book renders the same beat as pure non-verbal staging: fighters square off and face each other in fighting stances [S6], with Fighter A meeting Fighter B in the center of the ring [S8].

So, read as a corpus question: the books treat the face-off as a ritualized confrontation that establishes distance, posture, and the starting point of combat — not as a named cinematic device. If you meant the John Woo film, a treatise on “face-off” scenes in cinema, or the FACS/acting sense of the term, that specific content is not in the evidence.

results.question: What does the book say about affect, fatigue, and injury are control states?
results.answer:
The handbook's core claim is that affect, fatigue, and injury are **control states**: they operate inside the control loop and must change later action selection and execution, rather than functioning as adjectives appended after the choreography is chosen [S2]. What follows from that principle is that each state is specified as measurable parameters plus behavioral consequences, so downstream movement, attention, and risk-taking actually respond to the character's condition.

| State | How the handbook represents it | What it changes downstream | Supporting corpus material |
|---|---|---|---|
| Affect | Valence, arousal, dominance/control, updated by appraisal [S1][S2] | Attention, recovery quality, risk tolerance [S2] | Circumplex model of affect: 2-D structure, arousal–sympathetic correlation [S8][S11] |
| Injury | Region, pain, severity, capacity multipliers, compensations [S3] | Load acceptance, stance timing, trunk lean [S3] | Stage/screen combat: symmetry vs. contortion, vocal pitch shifts [S14][S10] |
| Fatigue | Global exertion + local capacity + coordination effects [S4] | Step-width variability, stabilization time, trunk contribution [S4] | No cinematic material — handbook formalization only |

## Affect is an appraisal layer, not an emotion label

In the layered representation, affect occupies Layer B as a continuous trajectory on valence, arousal, and dominance. It answers whether the character's experience becomes more positive or negative, activated or calm, empowered or overwhelmed — and it is built for interpolation and temporal arcs. Yet it stays **underdetermined**: the same high-arousal negative state could be performed as fear, anger, pain, or disgust depending on appraisal, context, and action tendencies [S1].

The handbook models this with an appraisal update that rewrites affect and declares concrete behavioral effects. In its worked example, an expected interception fails and the north lane opens; appraisal lands at goal congruence −0.72 with controllability 0.34 and certainty 0.61; affect moves from {−0.20, 0.58, 0.56} to {−0.48, 0.76, 0.38}; and the character's attention narrows toward the exit lane, recovery becomes urgent but less mechanically clean, and risk tolerance rises for one recovery attempt [S2]. The valence–arousal two-factor structure behind this is empirically well supported — psychometric studies consistently reproduce it, and arousal correlates with sympathetic nervous system activity [S8][S11] — but the handbook warns against compiling "anger = always faster" or "fear = always retreat": kinematic cues to emotion exist at population level, not as a deterministic universal mapping, with character, culture, task, injury, and tactical intent as moderators [S15].

## Injury means mechanical consequences plus how the body reads on screen

An injury object must carry mechanical consequences and compensations rather than a mere label: region, structural status, pain, severity, and capacity multipliers for load acceptance, flexion tolerance, and push-off. In the handbook's knee-injury example, the character compensates by favoring the right leg, shortening the left stance interval, and increasing trunk lean during emergency recovery — with the explicit caveat that this is dramatic annotation, not clinical measurement, so confidence sits at 0.70 [S3].

The cinematic craft sources show how such states become legible to an audience. In screen combat, **control is the visible currency**: a body in natural, symmetric positions reads as deliberate, while contorted, non-matching shapes read as being moved against one's will — flinch, squirm, spasm. Hence the chalk-outline rule that a symmetrical crime-scene pose is comedy while twisted, awkward limbs signal that something is wrong; the actor deliberately contorts so the pain reads while the performance stays safely fake [S14]. Stage combat adds a vocal channel: pain alters breath and the voice's pitch, rhythm, quality, resonance, and intensity — injuries near the body's center tend to lower pitch, peripheral ones raise it, and adrenaline can mask an injury entirely [S10].

## Fatigue is capacity, best compiled as a state variable

Fatigue factors into global exertion (RPE, breath-cycle length, recovery rate) and local capacity per limb or shoulder, with coordination effects such as increased step-width variability, longer stabilization after hard redirection, and greater trunk contribution when the right shoulder is taxed [S4]. The handbook outlines a compiler state — f<sub>r,t+Δ</sub> = clamp(f<sub>r,t</sub> + work<sub>r,t</sub> + impact<sub>r,t</sub> − recovery<sub>r,t</sub>, 0, 1), where f is fatigue, not remaining capacity — while warning that the work, impact, and recovery terms must be calibrated and "not inferred reliably from prose alone" [S6]. One gap: the retrieved corpus contains no cinematic case study of fatigue as a control state; the screen and stage craft material covers pain and injury, not fatigue. The movement-state vocabulary in the corpus — the six effort states (mobile, stable, remote, rhythm, dream, awake), each a two-factor combination [S7][S13] — describes expressive execution at a similar granularity, but it is a separate scheme from the handbook's control states.

What unites all three is that each is underdetermined as a label and overdetermined as a constraint: the same affect can read as fear or anger, the same injury as spasm or deliberate effort. So the handbook's prescription is to encode appraisal, mechanical consequences, and compensations — and let those control states reshape selection and execution downstream.

results.question: What does the book say about movement of an object with a background?
results.answer:
The book — really, several of your filmmaking sources — treats object movement as something you can only read *against a background*. Movement is never absolute in the frame; it's defined by the object's changing position relative to the frame line and the scenery behind it.

## The core principle

An object is "moving" only when its position changes in relation to the frame, and its motion is gauged by comparison with a second, stationary reference point — a concept the sources call **relative movement** [S3][S8]. Once motion is established, it can be categorized four ways: direction, quality, scale, and speed [S5]. The strongest possible contrast to this is **no movement at all** — tableau staging, where the stationary arrangement of objects carries the scene [S2].

## Backgrounds can create or steal movement

The background isn't passive scenery; it actively shapes what the viewer perceives. In **induced movement**, a moving object transfers its movement to a nearby stationary object, so the stationary thing appears to move and the moving thing appears frozen [S1]. A practical example: when the camera pans to follow a car driving in a circle, the trees in the background stream in the opposite direction of the pan. The trees' apparent movement reveals the car is moving — even though the car itself stays fixed in relation to the frame. That's background-generated *apparent movement* transferred to the subject, with no true relative movement at all [S13].

## Techniques and their purposes

- **Motion parallax** — move actors or camera so players travel between, behind, or past foreground objects, partially covered at intervals. The different travel speeds of objects at different distances convey position and depth to the viewer [S10].
- **Match moving** — when the foreground camera moves, the background must move correspondingly; in compositing, tracking data is extracted from the foreground shot and applied to the background so they lock together [S6][S4].
- **Tracking alongside** — the simplest motivated camera move, which emphasizes the moving background and the sweep of the motion rather than the subject alone [S14].
- **Telephoto circle** — a circular tracking move around a static subject with a long lens makes the background appear to revolve quickly behind them, as if the world is spinning out of control. The effect strengthens with more distance between subject and background, faster camera moves, and longer focal lengths — and it's ideal for visualizing a character's psychological breakdown or inner turmoil [S9].
- **Continuity of tracks** — movement begun in one shot can be continued in the next, with the second shot's track starting where the first ended, creating a continuum of movement across cuts [S7][S15].

The through-line across all of these: filmmakers rarely worry about the object's movement alone — they control what the *background* does, through camera moves, lens choice, and parallax, to sell a movement, exaggerate it, or give it psychological meaning. The forest example is the cleanest summary: the car doesn't move in the frame at all, yet the background makes you feel its motion [S13].

results.question: What does the book say about sound editing?
results.answer:
Across the sources, sound editing is described as the post-production craft of building the film's soundtrack around each scene's narrative point, with believability as its highest priority — because viewers process sound faster than pictures, an unconvincing track undermines the visuals and breaks audience involvement [S1][S11]. The sound edit is considered more elaborate and decision-heavy than the picture edit, and wrong choices can readily sabotage what the images achieve [S1].

**Core goals**

The editor's first task is to determine the narrative point of the scene and then surround it with sound [S1]. Narrative clarity and believability are the stated primary goals of the first phase of the edit [S11], and the sources repeatedly stress that without an effective sound track, the visuals will not succeed [S1].

**How the work proceeds**

- During the **rough cut**, only the tracks needed for dramatic decisions are used — typically dialogue and scratch music. After picture lock, the editor and sound designer build the multi-track sound design one track at a time [S7].
- A film's **sound design** is an aural universe of layered dialogue, sound effects, music, ambient atmospheres, and sometimes voice-overs [S7]. These are assembled, synced, and grouped into tracks — usually 6–16 for simple films — then equalized and mixed down to a master, from stereo up to 5.1 surround for cinema [S7]. Feature-film mixes can reach up to 60 tracks [S13].
- The mix itself gives the editor expressive control: separating sound effects lets the mixer fade one out while fading another in, and a continuing sound carried over two disparate visuals implies a link between shots or scenes, so the mix can separate or connect, and can imply the passage or continuity of time [S13].
- Editors also **acquire and create new audio** during post-production — the sources list sounds gathered to augment or even replace production audio, generating a more realistic "reality" for the narrative [S9]. Tools like the Fairlight page in DaVinci Resolve are highlighted as integrating sound work directly into the editing application [S10].

**Role in filmmaking**

Sound works on audiences at physiological, psychological, and emotional levels, which is why "silent" films were never meant to be silent — music was always arranged to accompany screenings [S5]. The **sound designer's creative role** is compared to that of the director of photography for picture, overseeing the overall acoustic experience and the individual tracks of dialogue, ambience, hard sound effects, and foley [S6]. Historically, early sound cinema was so hard to record and synchronize that it constrained editing itself — dialog scenes on disk couldn't be cut without losing sync, and editing was restricted to silent sequences until rerecording and multiple-camera techniques arrived [S14].

The one extended example in the material is *The Battle of Algiers* (1966), where authenticity is central to audience involvement and the narrative point is supported by the surrounding sound [S1].

Two details are named but cut off in the retrieved excerpts: sound effects are said to fall into four main categories, but those categories are not listed in what was retrieved [S8], and sound editing is described as a time for manipulating speed and pitch [S2] without the surrounding explanation.

results.question: What does the book say about write radio sparely?
results.answer:
The book's core advice on radio copy is blunt: underwrite. Overwriting is the most common mistake people make in radio, and the prescription is the opposite — "Be a genius. Underwrite." [S3]

It gives three reasons for writing sparely. First, time: a 60-second spot is a house, but a :30 is a tent — and since most radio spots are promotional, clients often add their own tags at the end, which cuts even deeper into the running time [S1]. Second, performance: sparse copy lets the voice talent read slowly, quietly, one word at a time [S2]. Third, silence itself: bare-bones execution leaps out of the radio, because silence is to radio what white space is to print — it enlarges the idea it surrounds [S8].

The practical technique is to handle the mandatories first. For something like a bank spot that must end with a batch of legal language, write that required copy as sparely as possible, time it, and whatever time remains is where the creative has to fit [S3]. The one exception is when the concept itself demands a lot of words and fast action — then density is justified [S2]. But the default is spare, and the book's rule of thumb is to let the silence carry some of the selling.
